title: Google books Blue Origin’s New Glenn to launch its AI satellites in 2029
excerpt: Google has picked Blue Origin's New Glenn to launch Project Suncatcher satellites carrying its AI chips in early 2029. Each is roughly a server rack.
content_html:
Google has signed Blue Origin to launch satellites for Project Suncatcher, its research into AI data centres in space, on a New Glenn rocket in the first quarter of 2029. Each satellite carries Google TPUs and roughly a data centre rack of computing power.

Google has booked Blue Origin’s New Glenn rocket to launch satellites carrying its AI chips in the first quarter of 2029, the company announced on Thursday. It will be the first dedicated heavy-lift launch for Project Suncatcher, Google’s research into data centres in space. New Glenn has been grounded since it exploded during a test in May, and its return to flight has slipped to January.

The solar-powered satellites will carry Google’s Tensor Processing Units, the chips it designs for AI. Each is meant to hold roughly a data centre rack’s worth of computing. They will fly in a sun-synchronous orbit, where they get sunlight almost all the time.

Google says solar panels in orbit can produce up to eight times more power than on Earth. That is the pitch, as AI data centres strain power grids on the ground. Neither company disclosed the value of the deal.

Suncatcher’s first prototype, built by Planet, reached orbit in October and ran Gemma 4 in space, sending back a haiku. Google is now testing how its chips cope with heat and radiation. It plans to link two satellites in 2027, before the bigger New Glenn launch.

The hardest problems remain unsolved. Chips in space cannot be cooled by air, and satellites must stay in tight formation to talk to each other by laser.

Google is not alone. Starcloud raised $170M in March to build data centres in orbit. SpaceX, Blue Origin’s rival, warned in its IPO filing that its own orbital data centres may never work.
